It's incredible to me how low profile this is in the media here in the US. This has huge implications on a global scale and it has so far been limited to financial news outlets.

You would think that most of the network news channels would be foaming at the mouth for a "sky is falling" situation to report on.

The China market is highly insulated. They don't buy a lot of US and EU goods if any. Outside investing became legal only a few years ago. If the Chinese market got hit by a meteor it would have a surprisingly small impact on global economies considering their GDP and size. I share your disapointment at coverage. Nearly all English news sites say the exact same thing, no real discussions and prediction of the future or possible impacts.

Is this common knowledge? Peat moss is very unsustainable but coconut coir is a great alternative.

Yes, it is very common knowledge.

Even the post you have linked to is 9 years old.
I knew peat harvest was unsustainable, but didn't know about coconut coir. I've only seen coconut fibres used as linings for planters and baskets. I wonder how the coir does for lawns?
Can you just purchase coconut coir at gardening places?
Yes it usually comes as a compressed brick. It's fun pulling it apart.

Unfortunately, most coconut coir comes from Sri Lanka and there it is rinsed repeatedly with freshwater which is a huge burden on the environment. Even organic coconut coir needs freshwater to be rinsed.

As a result your coconut coir is poor in nutrients which is ok for sprouts and some plants, but often fertilizer needs to be supplemented.

It was only recently when I learned about the use of coco coir as an alternative to peat moss. For me, it wasn't common knowledge. I've been using peat moss for making my own DIY potting soil mixes. I think the popularity of square foot gardening contributes to the use of peat moss as it is listed in the book as part of the "Mel's Mix" soil mix.
